section.title: Ryan Olsen: Instagram Stories, Fast Promotions, and Small Teams
section.deck: Ryan Olsen traces a path from a failed Facebook interview to leading iOS on Instagram Stories, rapid promotions, a tech lead director role and a startup, arguing for small teams, strong designers and building for people.

blocks.text: Ryan Olsen, a former Instagram principal engineer (IC8) who now co-founded the company behind the social app Retro, argues from his own career that small teams with full ownership move fastest, that product engineers multiply their impact by pairing with a strong designer and building their own ideas, and that promotions are an incentive system rather than a pure measure of output. The host walks him through a failed Facebook interview, a Flipboard internship, the White Out redesign, Instagram Stories, IGTV, IG Labs, a stint as tech lead director, and the move to a startup. Editorial note: every claim below is Olsen's recollection or opinion, and the captions are auto-generated, so some names are normalized.
blocks.heading: Olsen's view: go small, build for people, and bet on yourself

blocks.question: In 2011 Olsen interviewed at Facebook and failed. What was that experience like?
answer: Olsen says he badly wanted Facebook and was extremely nervous. The interviewer turned a laptop toward him to code on, and Olsen says his hands shook so hard the keys audibly rattled, which started a feedback loop of pounding heart and worsening nerves.

The question was an "engram buckets" problem, as the captions render it, with a simple dictionary-based solution. The solution did not come to him and he wrote a horrendous triple-nested loop. The interviewer cut the session short and said he would not make it at Facebook, which Olsen calls a knife to the heart. He says he would never end an interview early as an interviewer. He adds that the question was later banned at Facebook.
Olsen was down for a while, then bounced back, had a good career at Facebook, and feels he proved the interviewer wrong. He never learned the interviewer's name.

followups.question: The host says this shows how broken the interview process is, since a high performer failed it. Does Olsen agree?
answer: Olsen says he has always struggled with LeetCode-style interviews and wanted to change them at Facebook, but the process there is a machine spread across a big company. He enjoys that at his own company he does not have to do things he disagrees with.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: After the failed Facebook interview, how did Olsen end up as an intern at Flipboard, and what was that like?
answer: A couple of months later Olsen interviewed with Amazon by phone, felt far more comfortable, and received an exploding offer: a call on Friday, an answer due Monday. He was prepared to accept, but an investor friend who had offered to connect him with startups told him not to take it yet. That Sunday the friend emailed an introduction to a Flipboard co-founder named Evan.

Olsen did not want another interview call but is glad he answered. By his account, Evan had worked at Apple on the core of iOS, wrote the UIViewController class, and taught the Stanford course CS 193P, which was on iTunes and was how Olsen learned iOS. Flipboard suddenly looked more interesting than Amazon.

That summer Flipboard had about 50 people and roughly four interns. Olsen describes an extremely high density of talent, including people who had written iOS frameworks at Apple. An intern beside him had written Apple's push notifications framework and told stories about a clock-app time zone bug that left alarms silent around New Year. Olsen says he learned a great deal about iOS and building product.

Dylan Field, who founded Figma, ended his internship midway through the summer and founded it then. Olsen questioned whether to return and finish his last year of school and is ultimately glad he did, though it felt like a moment he might miss.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: Dylan Field of Figma and Devon Finzer, a later OpenSea founder, were both interns. Did Olsen notice traits that foreshadowed their success?
answer: Olsen says both were plainly determined to start companies, unlike his university classmates, whose highest aspiration was a job at big tech. There was a lot of talk about ideas.

On Figma's early days, he says the founders had one real insight: WebGL was a new technology that would enable new things on the web, and Dylan's co-founder was a skilled early WebGL engineer. They went through iterations not aimed at designers, including, as Dylan once described it, a meme generator app for about a week. Olsen's view is that it took time to find the use case and customer, but they stuck to the belief that the technology would change things.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: While at Flipboard, Olsen built a successful open-source project, with first commits in 2014. What is the story behind it?
answer: During the internship Olsen built internal debugging tools for Flipboard's iOS app. It was his first deep work in Objective-C, and he liked that the language is compiled but has a runtime exposing classes, methods, state and properties while the app runs. The first version, called FLTweaker internally, inspected and tweaked app state on demand.

He kept iterating on it on nights and weekends while the three-to-five-person iOS team built Flipboard. Colleagues found it useful for seeing network requests and the file system. Everyone agreed to open-source it, and it became, in his words, one of the more popular iOS debugging tools, used at Facebook and Instagram. He has been a less active maintainer since a couple of years into Instagram, and an engineer named Tanner took it over.

followups.question: The host asks whether open-sourcing the tool had an unexpected effect on Olsen's career.
answer: Olsen says it did in some ways, though less than he hoped. At his Instagram interview none of his interviewers wanted to look at the released code; they wanted a phone-number-sorting problem, which he found frustrating. But a Facebook iOS engineer outside the interview loop, who Olsen says may have created the original Xcode project for the Facebook app, got him to interview after seeing the tool and advocated for him in candidate review.

Having been very nervous in the internship interview, Olsen took a prescribed beta blocker for the full-time interview. He describes it as blocking adrenaline, so the pounding heart and sweaty palms never start a spiral, and says performers such as comedians use it too. Editorial note: this is one person's account, not medical advice.

The loop was still LeetCode-style, which he does not do well at, with a few strong-hire results and probably a few no-hires. He joined at IC4, one level above a new grad, and believes he was underleveled partly because of that loop.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

followups.question: The host asks whether the beta blocker removed the nerves entirely or only helped a little.
answer: Olsen has used them only a handful of times. He says they pretty much removed the physical effects, though a person can still be in their own head about what they are saying.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: What was the Instagram iOS team like when Olsen joined, and what did he do first?
answer: About ten iOS engineers worked on Instagram when Olsen arrived. As the story was told to him, the team had been about twenty before an internal war over the codebase. The manager, Scott Goodson, had built Async Display Kit for Facebook's Paper app; some engineers backed it, others wanted vanilla iOS. Olsen says the factions fought until nobody won and many left, so few engineers had been there more than six months to a year, and there was low-hanging fruit.

His first move was profiling cold start with Xcode's time profiler. The startup path did work for the profile tab that most people never open, and deferring it cut cold start by about 20 percent. Next, AFNetworking was built with assertions on and so crashed the app on benign failures such as a network error. A one-line change to block assertions cut the crash rate by 80 percent, he says.
That earned him the axe, a weekly award for outsized impact open to any function, in the form of a large physical axe carried around for a week.

followups.question: Where did the axe tradition come from?
answer: Olsen's account is that a men's magazine asked the founders for a holiday gift guide, they listed a bespoke axe, and an investor read it and sent them a huge one. Facebook security disliked a weapon in the office, so it was mounted on a plaque.

Later in his time there the tradition was ended deliberately, apparently because people felt excluded by a weapon being passed around. Olsen was sad, since the founders were gone and it felt like early Instagram culture being swept under the rug.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: What was the story behind White Out, the big Instagram redesign?
answer: A couple of months after joining, Olsen heard that a new app icon, which became very controversial, was coming with a visual refresh. He told his manager he had to work on it and says he maneuvered himself onto the project. He spent two or three months in a conference-room war room with the main designer, passing the phone back and forth screen by screen.

They built a new color palette and icons to put the focus on photos and videos and take the color out of the chrome, which at the time was dark blue and black. Olsen says it is basically how Instagram looks today.

followups.question: Was it a gated launch or all at once?
answer: Olsen says A/B testing was new at Instagram, and the CTO and co-founder, Mike Krieger, told him not to bother and just to build and ship. Having seen long-lived branches go badly, such as direct messaging, Olsen put the redesign, which touched every surface, behind a feature flag and kept merging, using semantic colors so code said "icon color" and a function switched between old and new design.

That opened up testing, with a 2 percent holdout on the old design. The night before launch, with the app submitted and champagne ready, someone on Facebook's executive team demanded A/B tests up front because a Facebook redesign had gone badly. Olsen backed things out and resubmitted around 1 a.m.; it tested well, but the delay crushed the planned launch.

His takeaway is that testing is valuable, including for onboarding at his startup, but for high-level product direction he prefers a strong opinion over letting data alone decide. Too much experimentation risks incrementalism: easy 1 percent wins but never a 50 percent jump.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

followups.question: The host notes the other risk: that the product taste is off and people hate the change. How did that play out?
answer: Olsen says the redesign felt right internally and was fine, but the icon was more controversial and people hated it at launch. He stopped looking at Twitter after what was meant to be a celebratory day. He attributes this to change being hard, people feeling ownership of their home screens, and a more bleeding-edge flat-and-gradient look in an era of skeuomorphic icons.
The data nonetheless showed the icon change materially raised daily app opens, and he says he has seen icon visibility affect opens with Retro too.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

followups.question: The host links this to Thomas Dimson's work on ranked versus chronological feeds, where public perception differed from usage. Was Olsen persuaded by ranking?
answer: Olsen says ranking shipped around the same time and he was skeptical at first. What changed his mind was that people with the ranked feed shared more themselves, partly because ranking showed them friends more often. He adds that the story may differ today. That fit the mission he liked, capturing and sharing the world's moments, so more creation looked like a good sign.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: The host notes that Olsen credited finding an amazing designer. How did he find one, and what makes a designer great?
answer: Olsen says he has tried to be the engineer that top designers want to work with. At companies like this, designers' work can flow through you, and a product engineer's impact is multiplied by building a good working relationship with a strong designer.

followups.question: Why a designer rather than a very senior engineer?
answer: Olsen distinguishes roles. For product engineers building user-facing features, the best pairing is a designer. In an infrastructure role the analogy is a super-senior engineer with great ideas, and being the engineer they want to work with.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: White Out was in 2016, the same year Olsen helped build Stories. What is the story of building Stories?
answer: After the redesign, Olsen's team moved to New York and he declined to relocate, so he joined Search and Explore. Within weeks a friend who led the creation team and the project that became Stories quit, and his manager said it was an important effort and a good opportunity. Olsen believed in it because Instagram felt, in some ways, like it was dying: everyday sharing among normal people was evaporating, replaced by creators and influencers, with some going to Snapchat's ephemeral format. The task was to make normal people comfortable sharing on Instagram again.

One of his first moves as iOS lead was to cut the team substantially. The project had churned through directions that did not feel good, and there was too little real work for the people on it. The core was Olsen and one other iOS engineer, plus help from other iOS engineers, two Android engineers, and only half the time of someone from infrastructure. Full ownership meant no stepping on toes and faster decisions. His summary: to go fast, go small.

They built it in two to three months. Olsen says he worked 16 to 18 hour days, seven days a week, driving home to San Francisco at 1 or 2 a.m. rather than sleeping in the office, which he now calls silly. It was intense but fun, the team bonded, and the product manager is now his co-founder. They felt like the underdog against Snapchat.

followups.question: What did the Instagram version do better than Snapchat?
answer: Olsen says Instagram had an unfair advantage: people already had their friends there but lacked the right outlet to share with them. Once that existed, the outflow of everyday sharing to Snapchat stopped. He gives Snapchat full credit for the container, a 24-hour, full-screen, immersive format, but says Instagram added touches such as tapping left to go back.

He also built hold-to-pause after using an early autoplaying build that moved too fast and instinctively pressing his thumb to stop it. His advice to engineers he mentors is that product engineers can build their own ideas, so they should build and put them in front of people.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

followups.question: The host asks about the 16 to 18 hour days. Did he ever feel a person could not survive that?
answer: Olsen says it probably was not 16 to 18 every day, but it was a lot, and he sacrificed other parts of life. A serious rock climber who had competed in World Cups on the US team, he effectively gave that up. It was a unique chance to build something going to hundreds of millions of people, and he loved seeing someone on the Caltrain using a feature he had built a week earlier. He calls the pace unsustainable but says it can make sense in stints.

Olsen thinks Stories was better executed than the efforts at Facebook and Messenger, partly from the team's care. He feared it would crash and burn and was surprised when people called it polished. Delivering on a tight timeline with that craft, he says, helped him get onto the most interesting projects afterward.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: Olsen went from IC4 to IC6 in two consecutive halves. What happened?
answer: Olsen says the promotion cycle was in July while Stories shipped in early August, so calibrations took place mid-crunch. He believes managers were cautious, and he felt fairly confident he had been underleveled when hired, having not known much about levels. His Android counterpart, Will Bailey, who he says was tech lead for Stories and an IC8, got him into meetings with Mike and Kevin and set an example of a successful product engineer. Seeing IC4 beside IC8 on similar roles opened his eyes to leveling.

He told his manager, Eddie, a director to whom he reported directly because of the project, that he had been misleveled and should go from four to six that cycle. Olsen credits him with not brushing it off: he checked with HR, who said it had been done twice in company history and both people left quickly. Olsen says he mainly wanted to seed the idea that his correct level was higher. He got IC5 for White Out and infrastructure work, then IC6 for Stories.

His broader point is that levels and promotions are an incentive system. He thinks there is a real effort to make them fair, but promotions can be delayed so two do not come in quick succession, because it is a carrot dangled in front of people.

followups.question: The host asks how strong performance gave Olsen the freedom to choose projects.
answer: Olsen says it showed that if he is put on a project he will do well, so when a new effort starts the company picks people who did well on earlier ones. He calls himself lucky, with good execution setting him up for later chances. When the host notes that Threads reused this model of pulling proven people into a small team, Olsen agrees it is a fun environment.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: The next promotion, to IC7, came through IGTV. What was that project?
answer: Olsen says IGTV began with Kevin, the CEO, and a designer, Ian, who unveiled a vision for longer-form, mobile-native vertical video at an end-of-year all-hands. Olsen wanted to work on it. He says recent antitrust litigation against Facebook shows tensions between the two companies then; his team was told for a while not to work on it, and he sees it as roughly the end of the founders' time.

The team was small: Olsen, Will Bailey and Thomas Dimson as iOS, Android and server leads, each with one or two others per platform. The product no longer exists and did not do well. Olsen thinks it held part of the future, since vertical video is now central, but it tried to put YouTube-style long-form content in a vertical format and people were not producing high-quality long-form vertical video.

The team tried AI techniques to reformat landscape video for vertical, on which Olsen holds a patent, but creators were horrified. Pushing creators to make original vertical long-form never produced the inventory, and Olsen sees some hubris in assuming Instagram could change what creators make. He believes it informed what shipped as Reels.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: The host asks what the antitrust angle is that Olsen mentioned.
answer: Olsen says internal communications made public through the antitrust suit, in which he understands the Justice Department is trying to unwind the Instagram acquisition, made some confusing events less confusing. His reading is that Instagram, small when acquired, grew into a peer of Facebook and the new popular kid. Stories was received better than Facebook's Stories, creating tension between the leaderships and concern that Instagram would cannibalize Facebook, which he says guided some strategy decisions.
The host recalls confusion at the time about cross-sharing from Facebook to Instagram being turned off and says Mark Zuckerberg's internal memo explains it. Olsen says he read the same material.

followups.question: How might Mark Zuckerberg view it today?
answer: Olsen wonders, since the communications suggest an understandable emotional attachment to Facebook, which Zuckerberg created, while Instagram was less his own thing. Olsen's own view is that the best outcome for a company owning both is to let them compete and improve each other, since stifling competition makes it likelier an outsider builds something better. He adds that he is armchair CEOing about someone running a multi-trillion-dollar company.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.label: Editorial note
blocks.text: The antitrust and Facebook-Instagram tensions in these two rounds are Olsen's and the host's readings of public litigation material and their own recollections. Olsen hedges (he thinks the Justice Department is the plaintiff), and this section does not verify them.

blocks.question: What is the story behind IG Labs, and how did it lead to the IC8 promotion?
answer: After IGTV, Olsen says he spent time in what Thomas Dimson calls the impact desert and was close to leaving. Reels was the new effort, and although his manager worked on it, he was fairly sure he did not want to work on passive video consumption.

Culture was changing too: the founders had left, new leadership came from Facebook, and old Instagram culture felt pushed out. Olsen pitched the new head of engineering on bringing back small teams, attention to craft and a wider scope, arguing the brand could support things beyond the existing app, such as location, maps and places ideas.

He started the group with a designer, Vivian Wong, at first just the two of them, as a Delta Force-style small, high-talent-density team for initiatives that did not fit cleanly into the org. By his account Instagram had grown so large that projects outside its structure were underinvested. The group tried many things, and much of it never shipped. He points to collaborative posts, with multiple authors on one post, as a lasting result and another of his patents. The group could also be pulled onto a major new initiative, which he says ended up being Threads.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: Olsen tried the rare tech lead director role. What was his thinking, and how did it go?
answer: Olsen says the role was rare at Facebook. It happened mostly because he had started the group, and it made more sense for him to manage the people than for his manager over Reels, who was less connected to their work. He was already representing them in calibrations, so the role was a formal recognition.

He says Facebook keeps individual contributors and management separate, and he disagrees. He cites Tesla as more flexible, with ICs often having reports and managers expected to be competent technical contributors. He holds what he calls a controversial opinion that senior engineers should code, citing Nassim Taleb's skin in the game: a senior IC who codes will not hand off an architecture as someone else's problem, and a manager close to day-to-day work operates better.

He also found an upside to a visible title. Facebook levels are private, which he likes for engineering debates because nobody can pull rank. In cross-functional work, such as shipping collaborative posts across many teams' PMs, a higher title gave a better baseline of credibility, since in a huge company you keep re-establishing reputation. He supported at least a public senior designation.

followups.question: The host says people warn that doing two jobs means you drown and neither career flourishes. What does Olsen say?
answer: Olsen says the criticism is probably correct. He was not optimizing for career and never intended to stay long: on Facebook's sentiment survey asking how long you plan to stay, he never put more than one year. He had no aspiration to reach IC9, which freed him to do what suited the team, and he knew he would not be fired for performance.
He also saw the cost firsthand: he believes his ratings were lower than they would have been as an IC, since he was exceeding as an IC but only meeting as a manager.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: What made Olsen leave Instagram and start Retro?
answer: In his last months at Instagram, Olsen talked with Nathan, now his co-founder, with whom he had built Stories. Nathan had gone to the Facebook side, started Facebook Dating, then worked on virtual reality. The close friends talked at a bar about building products and structuring a company differently, and about wanting to be in the driver's seat, but timing never aligned until both were ready. An investor friend and mentor, the one who connected him to Flipboard, told him it was time to bet on himself.

Olsen says the goal is a world-class product studio where great builders do the best work of their lives, making products people feel good after using, and also a successful business. Retro is the first product, not the reason the company exists.

Retro is a friends-focused social app. Olsen contrasts it with traditional social media, which he calls brain rot or entertainment. He says Instagram today shows him few people he knows and pulls him into short-form video that hijacks his attention. Retro is for staying up to date with people you know and looking back at your own photos. He says almost half of daily users post, much higher than he saw at Instagram, and that it became popular in Taiwan once it hit critical mass there. Editorial note: these usage claims are self-reported.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: What design philosophy did Retro take, and is it harder to grow when the app is less addictive?
answer: Olsen says a key decision was no ad-based business model. He does not think ads are evil, but ads combined with an algorithmic feed are a little evil because the incentives are misaligned: the app wants more of your time than you intended.

Growth is a real challenge. There are no creators; friending is mutual and private, with a limit of 250 friends, so no one can build an audience. He says Instagram grew partly through creators financially motivated to spread it, a path Retro lacks. He points to BeReal as a friends-only network that grew through a viral notification. His view is that growing a friends-only network is possible but harder, as is the business model, and the team is open about that. He frames it as an opinionated stance: some say to build what people want, but Retro bets that something better should exist as an option.
He says Retro coexists with Instagram; he still opens Instagram but gets sucked in less, and it has helped him break a phone habit.

followups.question: How does Retro make money without ads?
answer: Olsen says a small share of users take a premium subscription covering features that cost more to provide, such as video, since storage and bandwidth cost more than for photos. Posting video requires it, but he says the free version is good, and 93 percent of what people share on Retro is photos.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: Across learning, satisfaction and compensation, how has working on his own company compared with big tech?
answer: Olsen says compensation is quite a bit worse. He and Nathan pay themselves less than the employees and hold more ownership, which he thinks is right, accepting delayed pay in exchange for possible equity upside. Building a company was always what he wanted, and he was somewhat surprised to end up in big tech.

He says his time on interesting work is much higher now. In his later Instagram years he spent much of his work convincing layers above him that something should ship. He thinks more people worked on the app than needed to, which created gatekeeping over whether a team could ship and political wrangling about making someone feel an idea was theirs. He now spends none of his time on that; his only meeting is a daily one-hour standup, leaving nearly the whole day to build. His summary is that satisfaction and learning are higher and compensation lower.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: Would the company be better off if half the people were laid off?
answer: Olsen says yes. His team used to discuss a Thanos-style thought experiment in which half the company vanishes at random, and they often felt things would go better. He acknowledges that at Instagram's scale a 0.1 percent improvement can be worth hundreds of millions of dollars, but thinks the cost of each added person is underappreciated.

He cites organizational overhead of stakeholders, meetings and coordination, and the weight of more code. Just before leaving, a tool showed him spending more than four hours a day waiting for the app to build, because tooling had not kept up with how fast people wrote code. With a thousand engineers that slows everyone, though it is not noticeable per added person. When the team was ten and the app small, things were far easier, and he says White Out would be a massive project at Instagram today.

followups.question: The host raises Twitter's post-layoff experience as a case study. How does Olsen see it?
answer: Olsen says projections were that Twitter would fall over entirely after the cuts. His experience of it is somewhat buggy, but it keeps running, and he says he saw that its economics improved and it is now profitable, whereas it lost money through most of its history. Editorial note: these are Olsen's impressions, not verified figures.
followups.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: What stories show what made the founders and other colleagues exceptional?
answer: Olsen calls Mike Krieger something of a hero and says much of his thinking about engineering leadership came from him, including a simple-thing-first approach and attention to detail and craft. He describes a lead-from-the-front style in which Krieger never put himself above the team and jumped in wherever help was needed. At the end of Stories, a friend Olsen had borrowed from another Facebook team to build the drawing tools was pulled back partway through. Krieger said he would finish it, coded the neon brush, worked the same insane hours, and was up at 2 a.m. reviewing Olsen's diffs. Olsen says that informs how he leads teams.

Of Will Bailey, Olsen describes a strong product vision. During the dark days when Stories was spinning in circles, Bailey wrote a document outlining how the product should work, which Olsen later saw as essentially the five-year roadmap. He was an example of how a product-focused engineer can succeed and influence product direction, which Olsen says was valued more at Instagram than at Facebook, where he recalls bootcamp talk that juniors go to product teams and seniors to infrastructure.

He calls Thomas Dimson probably the smartest person he has met, and not in a savant way, since Dimson has social skills and understands people. Dimson started ranking at Instagram, with infrastructure skill but a product mindset. Olsen says he is interested in technology only as a means to create things for people, and sees Bailey and Dimson as similarly human-oriented, thinking about psychology and how products make people feel.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen

blocks.question: If Olsen could advise himself just after graduating, what would he say?
answer: Olsen says to invest in the tools of your time to build things for people. A new grad is not stuck as an iOS person or any one technology, so can pick up the latest tools. He believes that with the new AI tools new grads will probably be more skilled than senior engineers, who did not learn them natively.

He saw this with iOS: senior engineers were writing Java and the back end, and he stood out because iOS was the first thing he learned and he was eager and hungry. His advice is to learn the tools of your time, get good at them, and make good things for people. He says it is probably scary because it is hard to know how it will play out, and demand for junior engineers seems to be falling because of AI tools. But he believes anyone who gets very good at those tools will have roles.
blocks.speaker: Ryan Olsen
